Series::CalcAccessor::diff.strat¶

Back to Series::CalcAccessor API Reference

Signatures¶

// One state
Series::ItoDifferential Series::CalcAccessor::DiffAccessor::strat(
    const std::function<Series(const Series&)>& g,
    const Series& mu, const Series& sigma) const

// Two states
Series::ItoDifferential strat(
    const std::function<Series(const Series&, const Series&)>& g,
    const Series& mu, const Series& sigma, const Series::ItoState& other) const

// Any number of states, optional time argument
Series::ItoDifferential strat(const ItoFn& g, const Series& mu, const Series& sigma,
    const std::vector<Series::ItoState>& others, const Series::ItoOptions& options) const

// Converting a drift between the two conventions, one scalar process per element
Series strat_drift(const Series& ito_drift,
    const std::function<Series(const Series&)>& sigma) const
Series ito_drift(const Series& strat_drift,
    const std::function<Series(const Series&)>& sigma) const

What It Computes¶

A Stratonovich differential obeys the ordinary chain rule. If dX = μ dt + σ ∘ dW is written in Stratonovich form, then

drift      = g'(x) μ
diffusion  = g'(x) σ

with no second-order term. The same process in Itô form has a drift shifted by half of σσ':

μ_Stratonovich = μ_Itô − ½ σ(x) σ'(x)

so the same geometric Brownian motion dX = μX dt + σX dW (Itô) is dX = (μ − σ²/2) X dt + σX ∘ dW (Stratonovich). strat_drift and ito_drift convert a drift between the two, and they are exact inverses of each other.

The Stratonovich rule is also the right one for pathwise integration against a fractional Brownian motion with Hurst index above one half, which has zero quadratic variation.

The parameters, the result type and the shapes are those of diff.ito. Jumps are not accepted here: under the ordinary chain rule, a jump needs a rule for how it moves the state, which is what diff.marcus provides.

Parameters¶

  • g, mu, sigma, other, others, options: as for diff.ito.

  • ito_drift (for strat_drift) is the drift in Itô form, with the receiver’s shape.

  • strat_drift (for ito_drift) is the drift in Stratonovich form.

  • sigma (the callable) maps the state to the volatility at that state, with the receiver’s shape. It is differentiated by automatic differentiation to get σ'. Every element is its own one-dimensional process; the conversion does not mix elements.

Examples¶

Example 1. The ordinary chain rule. For g(x) = x² the Stratonovich drift is 2xμ with no σ² term, in contrast to diff.ito.

auto x = pluss::make_series({0.5, 1.0, -0.3});
auto mu = pluss::make_series({0.1, 0.2, -0.1});
auto sigma = pluss::make_series({0.3, 0.5, 0.2});
auto square = [](const pluss::Series& s) { return s.mul(s); };

auto strat = x.calc.diff.strat(square, mu, sigma);
auto ito = x.calc.diff.ito(square, mu, sigma);

std::cout << "strat drift " << strat.drift << "\n";
std::cout << "ito drift   " << ito.drift << "\n";
std::cout << "same diffusion " << strat.diffusion << "\n";

Output¶

strat drift pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[0.1, 0.4, 0.06]
ito drift   pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[0.19, 0.65, 0.1]
same diffusion pluss::Series(shape=[3,1], strides=[1,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[[0.3],
  [1],
  [-0.12]]

Example 2. Converting a drift. Geometric Brownian motion has Itô drift μx; the Stratonovich drift is (μ − σ²/2) x, and converting back recovers the original.

const double mu_c = 0.12, sg = 0.4;
auto x = pluss::make_series({0.5, 1.0, 2.0});
auto mu = x.mul(mu_c);
auto sigma_of = [sg](const pluss::Series& s) { return s.mul(sg); };

auto mu_strat = x.calc.diff.strat_drift(mu, sigma_of);
auto back = x.calc.diff.ito_drift(mu_strat, sigma_of);

std::cout << "Ito drift          " << mu << "\n";
std::cout << "Stratonovich drift " << mu_strat << "\n";
std::cout << "(mu - sigma^2/2) x " << (mu_c - 0.5 * sg * sg) * 0.5 << ", " << (mu_c - 0.5 * sg * sg) * 1.0 << ", "
          << (mu_c - 0.5 * sg * sg) * 2.0 << "\n";
std::cout << "round trip         " << back << "\n";

Output¶

Ito drift          pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[0.06, 0.12, 0.24]
Stratonovich drift pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[0.02, 0.04, 0.08]
(mu - sigma^2/2) x 0.02, 0.04, 0.08
round trip         pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[0.06, 0.12, 0.24]

Example 3. Both routes to d log X agree. The Itô route subtracts σ²/2 explicitly through the lemma; the Stratonovich route applies the ordinary chain rule to the converted drift.

const double mu_c = 0.12, sg = 0.4;
auto x = pluss::make_series({1.0});
auto mu = x.mul(mu_c);
auto sigma = x.mul(sg);
auto sigma_of = [sg](const pluss::Series& s) { return s.mul(sg); };
auto log_fn = [](const pluss::Series& s) { return s.log(); };

auto ito = x.calc.diff.ito(log_fn, mu, sigma);
auto strat = x.calc.diff.strat(log_fn, x.calc.diff.strat_drift(mu, sigma_of), sigma);

std::cout << "ito   drift " << ito.drift << " diffusion " << ito.diffusion << "\n";
std::cout << "strat drift " << strat.drift << " diffusion " << strat.diffusion << "\n";

Output¶

ito   drift pluss::Series(shape=[1], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=[0.04] diffusion pluss::Series(shape=[1,1], strides=[1,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=[[0.4]]
strat drift pluss::Series(shape=[1], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=[0.04] diffusion pluss::Series(shape=[1,1], strides=[1,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=[[0.4]]

Example 4. Two states under the ordinary chain rule: no covariation term.

auto x = pluss::make_series({2.0});
auto mu_x = pluss::make_series({0.05});
auto sigma_x = pluss::make_series({{0.3, 0.0}});
pluss::Series::ItoState y{pluss::make_series({1.5}), pluss::make_series({0.08}),
                          pluss::make_series({{0.24, 0.32}})};

auto d = x.calc.diff.strat(
    [](const pluss::Series& a, const pluss::Series& b) { return a.mul(b); }, mu_x, sigma_x, y);

std::cout << "drift " << d.drift << "  (= Y mu_x + X mu_y = " << 1.5 * 0.05 + 2.0 * 0.08 << ")\n";

Output¶

drift pluss::Series(shape=[1], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=[0.235]  (= Y mu_x + X mu_y = 0.235)

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • The drift you pass must be in Stratonovich form. A drift taken from an Itô model is off by ½ σσ'; convert it first with strat_drift.

  • strat_drift and ito_drift treat every element as its own scalar process. For a state with several coupled components the correction is not ½ σσ' per component.

Summary¶

diff.strat is the ordinary chain rule for Stratonovich processes, and strat_drift/ito_drift move a drift between the two conventions.
